subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What happens to an organism's surface area to volume ratio as it gets larger?
questions.explain: As an organism grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the surface area to volume ratio decreases.

questions.q: Why do large, multicellular animals need a transport system rather than relying on diffusion alone?
options: Their small surface area to volume ratio means diffusion is too slow to supply all cells
Diffusion does not occur inside animal cells
Their cells do not need oxygen or nutrients
A large surface area to volume ratio speeds diffusion up too much
questions.explain: Large animals have a small surface area to volume ratio and long diffusion distances, so a transport system is needed to move substances quickly to all cells.

questions.q: A cube-shaped block has sides of 2 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
questions.explain: Surface area = 6 x (2 x 2) = 24 cm2 and volume = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cm3, giving a ratio of 24:8 = 3:1.

questions.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.explain: The heart has four chambers: two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall?
questions.explain: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood at high pressure all around the body.

questions.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right ventricle?
options: It pumps blood only to the lungs, which are nearby
It must pump blood at high pressure to the whole body
It receives blood from the vena cava
It contains valves that the right ventricle lacks
questions.explain: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood around the entire body, so it needs more muscle to generate the higher pressure required.

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?
questions.explain: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'double circulatory system' in humans?
options: Blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body
There are two hearts working together
Blood flows in two directions along the same vessel
The heart beats twice as fast as other organs need
questions.explain: In a double circulation the blood travels through the heart once on the way to the lungs and again on the way to the rest of the body.

questions.q: Deoxygenated blood returning from the body through the vena cava first enters which chamber of the heart?
questions.explain: The vena cava empties deoxygenated blood into the right atrium, which then passes it to the right ventricle.

questions.q: Why can a blocked coronary artery lead to a heart attack?
options: The heart muscle is starved of oxygen and glucose
Blood can no longer leave the aorta
The valves are forced to close permanently
questions.explain: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself, so a blockage deprives that muscle of oxygen and glucose, damaging it.

questions.q: Which component of the blood is mainly responsible for transporting oxygen?
questions.explain: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin for transport around the body.

questions.q: How does having no nucleus and a biconcave shape help a red blood cell carry out its function?
options: It allows the cell to divide rapidly
It provides more space and surface area for haemoglobin and oxygen
It lets the cell fight pathogens more effectively
It helps the cell produce antibodies
questions.explain: Lacking a nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, and the biconcave shape increases surface area for absorbing oxygen.

questions.q: What is the main function of platelets in the blood?
questions.explain: Platelets are cell fragments that help the blood clot at wounds, sealing them and preventing blood loss and infection.

questions.q: Why do arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls?
options: To allow substances to diffuse in and out easily
To withstand and maintain the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart
To prevent the backflow of blood using valves
To slow the blood down for gas exchange
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood at high pressure from the heart, so their thick, elastic, muscular walls resist bursting and help maintain the pressure.

questions.q: How thick are the walls of a capillary?
options: The same thickness as an artery
The same thickness as a vein
questions.explain: Capillary walls are just one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance for the exchange of substances with tissues.

questions.q: Why do veins contain valves?
options: To speed the blood up to a high pressure
To prevent blood flowing backwards as it returns to the heart
To allow gas exchange with body cells
To pump the blood using muscle contraction
questions.explain: Blood in veins is under low pressure, so valves stop it flowing backwards and keep it moving towards the heart.

questions.q: A patient has a much lower than normal number of red blood cells. Which symptom would you most expect?
options: Tiredness caused by reduced oxygen transport
questions.explain: Fewer red blood cells means less haemoglobin to carry oxygen, so tissues receive less oxygen for respiration, causing tiredness.

questions.q: In which structures of the lungs does gas exchange take place?
questions.explain: Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli, the tiny air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between air and blood.

questions.q: Which feature of alveoli makes them well adapted for efficient gas exchange?
options: Thick, muscular walls to withstand pressure
A large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply
A single valve to control airflow
A dry lining to speed up diffusion
questions.explain: Alveoli have a large moist surface area, walls one cell thick and a rich capillary network, all of which maximise the rate of diffusion.

questions.q: When a person breathes in, what happens to the diaphragm?
options: It relaxes and moves up into a dome shape
It contracts and flattens, moving downwards
questions.explain: During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the chest and lowering the pressure so air is drawn in.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Biology (1BI0) specification; Exchange & Transport in Animals
